In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
M. bovis is a zoonotic pathogen with multiple wildlife reservoir hosts.

wildlife reservoirs of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) in general, and M. bovis in particular, are species with the ability to maintain the pathogen within their population, and to transmit the disease to cattle.
M. bovis can be transmitted from wildlife to cattle in some circumstances, and that wildlife reservoirs of this disease do exist.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that the epidemiological concepts of CCS and R0 are useful in identifying wildlife reservoir hosts of Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) in wildlife.

the epidemiological concepts of CCS and R0 are useful for predicting the existence of wildlife reservoirs of bovine tuberculosis, and the disease/pathogen characteristics of M. boves are also useful for identifying true reservoirs.
the epidemiological and disease characteristics of wildlife reservoir species are important for the design and implementation of control programmes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
wildlife reservoirs of bovine tuberculosis are not static.

wildlife reservoir hosts of tuberculosis are characterized by high M. bovis infection and shedding prevalence and low pathogenicity of M. bovs infection, which allows infected hosts to survive and transmit infection to other hosts.
